Chapter 7. Advanced Agents and Tools

In the previous chapters, we worked with a simple tool-calling agent that queries Databricks Vector Search to answer FAQ questions about Unity Airways. Agents, often referred to as AI agents, represent a major shift in GenAI application development. They can plan, invoke tools, observe results, and iterate based on feedback, enabling autonomous decision making and multistep reasoning. Because agents can adapt to complex scenarios without relying on predefined workflows, they can reduce tasks that once required time-consuming human intervention to just seconds. Customer service centers, for example, stand to benefit significantly when resolving traveler requests such as flight cancellations or specific flight changes.

The rapid adoption of agents has made it one of the most discussed topics in the AI community, with major companies and research institutions investing heavily in agent frameworks and tooling development such as Model Context Protocol (MCP). This push for better frameworks has helped MLflow 3.x grow faster thanks to active demand and contributors, as developers are looking for solid tools to manage and deploy these more complex GenAI applications.

This chapter delves further into agents to help our Unity Airways assistant perform more complex tasks for our users. We’ll look at the fundamentals of agent development, how to use LangGraph with MLflow and switch models from different providers, as well as how to create tools and integrate them with our agentic system. We’ll also do a pass on advanced features such as measuring tool performance, streaming responses, conversation history management, and multiagent orchestration strategies to finally wrap up on registering the agent with MLflow for later usage.

Developing Agents with MLflow

As we’ve covered throughout the book, MLflow 3.x is a practical tool for AI developers to navigate the complexity of AI development. It provides a standardized framework for prompt management, custom metric scorers, using tracing for observability, and many more features. Our previous agent could answer only predetermined FAQ questions for Unity Airways, but what if our customer would also like to check their up-to-date flight status? That agent wouldn’t be able to answer, as it is not connected to timely flight data. Let’s build a more complex and connected system to solve that problem.

What Are Agents, AI Agents, and Agentic AI?

An agent is usually referred to as a system that can choose or make decisions depending on some defined tasks and flow. In the past, these were often a set of decision rules and tools that were plugged together to perform tasks that end users might ask. Earlier generations of chatbots in customer services often used if-else rules for executing actions such as checking your flight booking (if the option was available) or checking the schedule for a flight (if you had mentioned the specific flight number, such as “JNC123,” in your question).

Today, AI agents infused with an LLM are more advanced systems that avoid the reliance on if-else hardcoded rules. They use an LLM to perform decision making by understanding the query and generating answers accordingly. Integrated with tools, the agent becomes a powerful system that can do various actions such as querying flight schedules from a database without needing the user to format input in a specific way. Usually, these architectures rely on a supervisor agent who will be deciding on what tools to call. This capability is a game changer, as it enables more fluidity and makes chatbots more natural, versatile, and relevant, broadening the possible uses for autonomous agents.

In a step further, these systems can be evolved into what’s called agentic AI systems, where the supervisor can choose between multiple AI agents to answer a query, splitting the questions and passing them to the right agent tuned especially for a certain type of query.

Figure 7-1 illustrates some examples of these three types of agents and how they could differ from one another within our Unity Airways use case.

As we progress in this example, we can see that the agentic AI system can process more complex user queries around flights, from asking what flights are scheduled (descriptive information) to asking for a recommendation on the best flight available (prescriptive information).

Warning

AI agents and agentic AI systems are more flexible and adaptable than rule-based chains systems, which makes them capable of handling a broader range of tasks. However, this means they can become less controlled or predictable, potentially allowing overly permissive behaviors. It is crucial to design appropriate guardrails and restrict certain options to maintain reliability and safety.

It’s important to consider your needs for a specific case before deciding which type of GenAI application to build. Adaptability and latency are usually two crucial indicators of what solution is best suited for a specific need. See Table 7-1 for more details on how to determine what is the best option to build.

Table 7-1. Main differences between agents and chains
FeaturesAgentsRule-based chains
Control flowDynamic flow; chooses next actions at runtime based on reasoning.Predefined, ordered steps; each call follows a fixed sequence.
AutonomyHigher autonomy; can plan, decide, and adapt within given goals/guardrails.Low autonomy; behavior is fully scripted by the developer.
AdaptabilitySuited to open-ended, variable tasks where inputs and paths are diverse.Best for predictable, repeatable tasks with stable requirements.
Consistency/reliabilityAgents are more dynamic and less reliable, as tools selection can change depending on how a query is phrased.Chains are more consistent by nature, as the same steps are processed in a deterministic way.
LatencyAgents usually have higher latency as the flow is more complex and the supervisor deciding on next action can be looped several times, causing extra latency. Latency can vary between 10 seconds to minutes. Chain latency can also vary, but it is usually consistent as the same flow is being processed. Having no supervisor also significantly reduces the latency as the action sequence is predefined.
FailuresAgentic systems can fail due to uncertainty in their decision making. The agent may select the wrong tools, loop unnecessarily, or accumulate small reasoning errors across multiple steps.Chains typically fail due to their sequential structure. Each step depends on the previous one, and formatting errors, unexpected outputs, or poor intermediate results can propagate in the pipeline, with little ability for adaptation.

Integration on MLflow

GenAI development relies on libraries and frameworks to orchestrate the various components needed to create AI agents. Just like software engineering and machine learning model development, having a repeatable management of the lifecycle of your agent development is fundamental.

MLflow 3.x integrates with many popular libraries (e.g., LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, DSPy, LlamaIndex) to support agent development and lifecycle. You can find all the supported package flavors in the official MLflow documentation.

On top of that, most of these orchestration packages have integration to model providers, and to Databricks as well, making it easy to swap models around for benchmarking purposes. For instance, when we create our flight assistant agent later, we will be using the databricks-langchain package to use a large language model provided by Databricks.

These packages are great tools that are used widely in AI development. MLflow adds capabilities on top for agent building, namely:

For debugging and iterating on agent prompts

Whether you build LangGraph agents or DSPy models, MLflow supports these with built-in automated tracing. Having this out of the box, as discussed in Chapter 5, is an asset in speeding up development and identifying potential bottlenecks or issues when debugging, especially when the flow of the agent is composed of multiple tool-calling steps or subagents. The prompt registry is also a good tool to version your prompt and keep iterating on your agent quality without fear of critical code regression, as it is easy to switch back to previous prompt versions.

For scaling agent evaluation

MLflow helps evaluate the different layers of agents you create. Any models logged with MLflow can be called in the evaluation functions and are model agnostic; in addition, the predict function can be customized through custom code to call any models or API. This is useful to get the entire output as traces to analyze for exhaustive tool evaluation, supervisor evaluation, and other formatting functions checks.

MLflow AI Gateway Interface for LLM Integration

As the number of available LLMs increases by the day, developers are faced with a broad and ever-growing array of choices for their projects. MLflow’s stance on that is to help integrate as many different LLM providers as possible to make your development easy. You’ll find many model providers being integrated to MLflow, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and others. These integrations mean that out-of-the-box traces are supported for these models, as well as auto-logging various parameters that matter for these specific models.

When using these different providers, another capability that MLflow offers to simplify development is to use MLflow AI Gateway to swap the models within your code.

MLflow AI Gateway is a centralized service that provides a unified and secure interface for interacting with multiple large language model providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI) within an organization. Figure 7-2 illustrates this. This simplifies secrets management by storing API keys in one place, reducing exposure across systems.

Following the same concept, Databricks offers Unity AI Gateway for enterprise use that streamlines the model serving and deployment experience on the Databricks platform. This gateway is built on top of MLflow One, with additional governance and cost control on top. It supports creating, updating, querying, and deleting endpoints for LLMs hosted on Databricks, as well as external models from different providers.

On top of the developers benefits of swapping models, using Unity AI Gateway provides governance and access control on the various LLMs, as it integrates with Unity Catalog. The gateway also has native capabilities like usage rate limits on user groups, possibility to attach guardrails, real-time tracking of usage, and inputs/outputs into tables for further analysis. If you are managing LLMs or AI models in production on Databricks, using the Unity AI Gateway is recommended for best scalability, security, and integration.

Now that we’ve discussed agents and MLflow integration of LLMs, let’s build some useful tools to integrate to an LLM for our Unity Airways AI agent.

For example, our unity Airways AI agent should be able to:

  • Answer frequently asked questions (as the example agent developed in Chapter 4).

  • Check user information and latest booking records to help the user confirm or edit their upcoming travel.

  • Retrieve real-time weather forecasts to alert on potential delays or cancellations in the user’s upcoming travel.

Creating Tools

Tools let our agent do more than just respond to a query using knowledge that the LLM was trained on. Providing the right tools can help the agent sift through data and execute specific actions that are relevant to a user query. To illustrate, here are some different tools being used in the industry:

Knowledge and database tools

These tools include connectors to query knowledge bases, vector databases, database access, execute SQL queries, and read or update records. These could be used to pass real-time flight arrival data to agents or retrieve passengers details, for instance.

API-based tools

These tools facilitate web searches, weather forecast retrieval, news feeds, and many more search possibilities.

Code execution tools

These tools enable dynamic code execution in various languages, such as Python or JavaScript, to process data, make charts and dashboards, or perform some actions.

Skills

While not technically tools themselves, skills help organize and specialize agent behavior for specific tasks or domains. Skills can dynamically and progressively provide the agent with focused instructions, workflows, context, or dedicated tool access depending on the user query. This allows the same agent to adapt its expertise for scenarios such as customer support, flight rebooking, loyalty program assistance, or operational troubleshooting.

MCP servers for platform integration

Often designed and offered by the platform itself, these tools permit the user to perform actions specific to the platform. Software used by the aviation industry could be used here to check on catering management or current aircraft location, for instance.

These tools can be developed in many ways, by simply wrapping the code into functions, using specific package integrations or MCP servers.

While both approaches allow agents to interact with external capabilities, they differ significantly in terms of standardization, reusability, and integration scope. Table 7-2 compares MCP servers and framework-specific Python tool integrations to help identify which approach best fits your architecture, team structure, and long-term scalability needs.

Table 7-2. Difference between using MCP servers versus other Python package tools
Tool typeMCP server
Other Python package Tool
(e.g., LangChain)
Core ideaStandard protocol for exposing tools/resources to LLMs in a model-friendly, discoverable way. You build a server with standardized input and output, and any compatible client or agent can consume it.Framework-specific integration. You write Python code that calls your REST API or perform needed operations and register it as a tool for a particular agent.
Who it’s forTeams that want one integration layer used by many agents, models, IDEs, and platforms.A single application team, where the integration is only meant for that project, pilot, or stack.
When to prefer itYou expect multiple agents, vendors, or projects to use the same capability. You want “plug-and-play” tools that work across ecosystems. Fast proof-of-concept or product feature in one codebase. You don’t need a generic, reusable “tool product” for others to consume.
Standardization and reuseHigh. One protocol, consistent tool schema, capability listing, and error semantics. Great for building an internal or public tool catalog others can plug into.Low. The integration is tightly coupled to LangChain abstractions and that project’s code. Reuse in other frameworks requires to glue code or create a shared package.
Operational overheadHigher up front, where you run a service (local or remote), handle deployment, versioning, and sometimes multitenant authentication.Code directly in the application.
Performance considerationsAdds one more hop and protocol translation, but lets tools be shared and optimized centrally. This adds to overall development complexity. Directly in-process with your agent, which makes fewer moving parts but less reusable.
Good for latency-sensitive, single-app workflows.

Essentially, we recommend using an MCP server when you want a standardized and reusable interface to your GenAI application that many agents and platforms can consume. This is usually more enterprise ready with proper governance and easier collaboration, but it is more time-consuming to set up. On the other hand, use a LangChain tool when you’re optimizing for one specific GenAI app or prototype and don’t need cross-platform reuse yet.

Now that we’ve seen the difference between MCP-based tools and Python packaged ones, let’s start adding new capabilities to the agent. We’ll create two tools, one for searching through text using Databricks Vector Search and another for looking up structured data using Unity Catalog functions, by using both custom code implementation and MCP server.

Vector Retriever Tool

As we’ve seen in earlier chapters, vector databases, such as Databricks Vector Search, are a handy way to help us find similar content quickly by querying documents related to our query. Now, instead of calling the retrieval search directly, we are going to wrap the search feature into a tool that our agent can use whenever it needs to find relevant information from our knowledge base.

To do that, we’re using the class VectorSearchRetrieverTool from the package databricks_langchain. This package contains various integrations to connect Databricks components with LangChain. Each tool has specific parameters that it needs to function properly. Here is an example: 

from databricks_langchain import VectorSearchRetrieverTool

# Use Databricks vector search index as tool
vector_retriever_tool = VectorSearchRetrieverTool(
    index_name="workspace.unity_airways.faq_index",
    num_results=5,
    tool_description="Search through Unity Airways frequently asked question (FAQ) about 
        flight cancellation, travel policies, and baggages security.")

This code creates a search tool that connects to our Unity Airways FAQ index. The index_name points to our FAQ data index name, deployed on Databricks; num_results=5 means it will return the top five most similar answers; and tool_​des⁠cription tells our agent what this tool is good for. tool_description must be as clear as possible, by describing what the tool can do, information on when to call it, and potential keywords that might be associated with the tool usage.

This is where clear naming and descriptions matter a lot. We want each tool to have its own clear purpose and not overlap with other tools, since having similar tools can confuse the supervisor agent about which one to pick to answer a user query.

Now, let’s call our tool with a query:

results = vector_retriever_tool.invoke({
   "query": "Can my battery pack be transported in cabin baggage?"
})

As queried, this returns the five most relevant documents to our input question in the MLflow Trace UI, as Figure 7-3 illustrates.

Structured Data Lookup Tool

For querying structured data like customer bookings on Databricks, we can use Unity Catalog functions as structured lookups functions. These functions can be used as tools to search through databases and return the queried data. Because these functions are user defined, they can include various preprocessing, filtering, or PII data masking, for example.

Let’s create a function to query specific customer booking records, using their email as input: 

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION workspace.unity_airways.lookup_customer_info(
 user_email STRING COMMENT 'Email of the customer whose info to look up.'
)
RETURNS TABLE
COMMENT 'Returns all metadata about a specific customer as a markdown table.'
RETURN (
   SELECT *
   FROM workspace.unity_airways.booking_records_dataset
   WHERE `primary_contact_email` LIKE user_email
)

We can see that user_email is the input of the function. Again, it’s important here to properly put a comment on the function to describe its usage. Now let’s test the function:

import pandas as pd
from unitycatalog.ai.core.databricks import DatabricksFunctionClient

client = DatabricksFunctionClient()
result = client.execute_function(
   function_name="workspace.unity_airways.lookup_customer_info",
   parameters={"user_email": 'alex.lim@example.com'}
)

pd.read_csv(result.value)

Testing this function code calls our lookup function and turns the results into an organized table format. When we search for a customer, such as Alex Lim, we get back all their booking details, flight history, and contact information in an easy-to-read format. Table 7-3 demonstrates this.

Now, let’s wrap this function into a tool. To do that, we use the UCFunctionToolkit from databricks_langchain. This will integrate the Unity Catalog functions into LangChain tools.

UCFunctionToolkit actually creates a list of tools (toolkit) by passing the function names you’d like to turn into tools to function_names. This toolkit has multiple tools inside that can be called individually by selecting tools by indices. Here is an example: 

from databricks_langchain import UCFunctionToolkit
from unitycatalog.ai.core.databricks import DatabricksFunctionClient

client = DatabricksFunctionClient()

# Create the toolkit with the function
uc_tool =  UCFunctionToolkit(
   function_names=["workspace.unity_airways.lookup_customer_info"], 
   client=client
)

# Use the uc_tool object
result = uc_tool.invoke({"user_email": "alex.lim@example.com"})
result

When we invoke the tool, it returns our data rows (see Table 7-3) about our customer flights, as expected.

Note

Databricks provides managed MCP servers for interfacing with Vector Search indexes and Unity Catalog functions. If you are using a Databricks Free Edition workspace, these managed MCP servers may not be available. You can substitute the managed MCP with external MCP servers.

API-Calling Tool

API-based tools are another type of popular tool, as they are versatile as long as an API exists to do the operation needed. In our case, let’s create a tool to get the next seven days of weather forecast based on the location from a free weather forecast API from Open-Meteo. It will help our AI agent check for weather constraints and potential inclement weather that could delay flight operations.

First, we create a BaseModel class to formalize our inputs. This helps make the input structured so that the LLM downstream will know what input to generate, which here is the latitude and longitude of our target forecast location: 

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Localization(BaseModel):
   latitude: float
   longitude: float

Our next function, get_weather_forecast, will call the Open-Meteo API with an http request using Python, format the returned weather data, and return it as a dictionary:

import openmeteo_requests

def get_weather_forecast(latitude: float, longitude: float) -> Dict[str, Any]:
   """
   Tool to fetch hourly weather forecast from Open-Meteo.
   """
   openmeteo = openmeteo_requests.Client()
   url = "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast"
   params = {
       "latitude": latitude, 
       "longitude":  longitude, 
       "hourly": ["temperature_2m", "rain", "precipitation_probability"],
   }
   responses = openmeteo.weather_api(url, params=params)   
   hourly = responses[0].Hourly()
   hourly_data = {
       "date": pd.date_range(
           start=pd.to_datetime(hourly.Time(), unit="s", utc=True),
           end=pd.to_datetime(hourly.TimeEnd(), unit="s", utc=True),
           freq=pd.Timedelta(seconds=hourly.Interval()),
           inclusive="left"
       ),
       "temperature_2m": hourly.Variables(0).ValuesAsNumpy(),
       "rain": hourly.Variables(1).ValuesAsNumpy(),
       "precipitation_probability": hourly.Variables(2).ValuesAsNumpy(),
   }   
   return hourly_data

The code inside the function is quite customizable. Any other API calls or logic such as formatting functions or Python code would actually work here as a tool.

Tip

While it is not shown in the preceding code example, it is a good practice to incorporate error handling within functions so that the LLM knows how to react in case of tool failure.

In the next step, we wrap this function into a LangChain StructuredTool as we’ve formalized our previous input format in the Localization class:

from langchain_core.tools import StructuredTool

weather_tool = StructuredTool(
    name="get_weather_forecast",
    func=get_weather_forecast,
    description="Get weather forecast given latitude and longitude.",
    args_schema=Localization,
)

As usual, it’s important to clarify the desired use of this tool by providing it with a name and a clear description. args_schema is the name of our structured input class. Technically, this tool could also be created with the Tool class instead of StructuredTool, but knowing how to secure the input type of our tool is a good practice to adopt, especially when using LLM, which can hallucinate and generate wrong input types.

Now, let’s try our tool by invoking it with the latitude and longitude of Singapore’s localization:

# Call the tool by passing an instance of the input schema
result = weather_tool.invoke({"latitude": 1.3667, "longitude": 103.8})
display(pd.DataFrame(result))

All good! It returns our weather forecast data for the next seven days in Singapore, as Table 7-4 shows.

Finally, let’s group all of our created tools into a list of tools so we can easily pass them to our agent later on:

tools = []
tools.extend([uc_tool])
tools.extend([vector_retriever_tool])
tools.extend([weather_tool])

Extending the Unity Airways Chatbot with Tools

Now that we’ve created our tools, let’s integrate them into our flight assistant agent. We recommend that you start with a small, well-defined toolset. By choosing a few high-impact actions (e.g., check status, fetch customer info, check weather forecast), we can design our code to create as much value as possible while keeping complexity low, and later iterate into a more extensive agentic system.

To integrate our various tools, we will be using the LangGraph package to orchestrate our agent workflow.

Note

As this book focuses on MLflow, we will keep our explanation on LangChain and LangGraph light. We recommend researching additional information on how to use these packages if needed and consulting the official documentation of the LangChain package.

At its core, LangGraph models agent workflows as graphs. You define the behavior of your agents using three key components:

State

A shared data structure that represents the current snapshot of your application. It can be any data type but is typically defined using a shared state schema.

Nodes

Functions that encode the logic of your agents. They receive the current state as input, perform some computation or side effect, and return an updated state.

Edges

Functions that determine which Node to execute next based on the current state. They can be conditional branches or fixed transitions.

Used together, these three components can form a workflow graph, as Figure 7-4 illustrates.

First, we start by defining our agent state. Here, our state is a dictionary of messages that will be passed from nodes to nodes. The messages field will contain the various message turns in the conversation. We’re also adding optional custom_inputs and custom_outputs, in case we want to pass some information that is needed to use for specific tools or relevant to the overall conversation: 

from typing import TypedDict, Annotated, Sequence, Optional, Any
from langchain_core.messages import BaseMessage
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages]
    custom_inputs: Optional[dict[str, Any]]
    custom_outputs: Optional[dict[str, Any]]

This AgentState will then be used throughout our tool-calling agent to keep track of the messages given by the user, tools, or LLM.

Next, let’s create our agent. For that, we create a function that will:

  • Use a model that is wrapped with the LangChain class of type LanguageModelLike.

  • Bind our recently created tools to our selected LLM using bind_tools().

  • Concatenate our prompt with the conversation messages using the preprocessor and pass this to our model in model_runnable.

  • Finally, create the StateGraph that will orchestrate the various nodes together.

The following code illustrates this procedure:

from langchain_core.language_models import LanguageModelLike
from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool
from langgraph.graph import END, StateGraph

def create_tool_calling_agent(
    model: LanguageModelLike,
    tools: Union[ToolNode, Sequence[BaseTool]],
    system_prompt: str,
):
    model = model.bind_tools(tools)
    preprocessor = RunnableLambda(lambda state: [{"role": "system", 
        "content": system_prompt}] + state["messages"])
   model_runnable = preprocessor | model

   workflow = StateGraph(AgentState)
   workflow.add_node("agent", RunnableLambda(call_model))
   workflow.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))
   workflow.set_entry_point("agent")
   workflow.add_conditional_edges(
       "agent",
       should_continue,
       {
           "continue": "tools",
           "end": END,
       },
   )
   workflow.add_edge("tools", "agent")

   return workflow.compile()

The creation of the StateGraph workflow has two principal nodes, the agent and the tools. The agent will call the model through the function call_model, while tools will use the ToolNode implementation.

You’ll notice that we’ve created two internal functions, should_continue and call_model, that are being called in our nodes and edges definitions.

The should_continue function in the LangGraph workflow is a routing function called immediately after the execution of the agent node, specifically used to determine the next step in the graph based on the agent’s latest action and output. Here is an example of its use:

# Define the function that determines which node to go to
def should_continue(state: AgentState):
       messages = state["messages"]
       last_message = messages[-1]
       # If there are function calls, continue; else, end
       if isinstance(last_message, AIMessage) and last_message.tool_calls:
           return "continue"
       else:
           return "end"

Every time the agent node finishes running (after the LLM produces its output, stored in the agent state), the graph invokes should_continue to decide if the workflow should continue to the tools node or go to the END state.

The call_model function uses the configured LLM by passing the current state and returns the LLM outputs:

   def call_model(
       state: AgentState,
       config: RunnableConfig,
   ):
       response = model_runnable.invoke(state, config)
       return {"messages": [response]}

Figure 7-5 illustrates the final workflow steps:

  1. The graph starts at the node agent, which calls the LLM via the function call_model.

  2. After the node agent completes, we go into an edge, where should_continue is called.

  3. If tool calls exist in the agent’s output passing in the state, the next node is tools. If not, the graph ends.

  4. After the node tools run, the state returns to the agent node to decide if another tool is needed or not, repeating until termination (back to step 3).

  5. If the graph ends, the final state of the graph is returned.

To create our agent, we can use our developed function. Pass it the LLM you’d like to use, the tools we’ve created earlier, and a prompt. For the agent to orchestrate the workflow and properly choose which tools to use, the agent will read the tools description given in each tool definition passed when using model.bind_tools(tools):

from databricks_langchain import ChatDatabricks

llm_endpoint_name = "databricks-gpt-oss-120b"
llm = ChatDatabricks(endpoint=llm_endpoint_name)

system_prompt = """You are a helpful flight assistant for Unity Airways, 
   capable of supporting users with their bookings and policy questions using 
   tools to retrieve information from Unity Airways knowledge bases.
"""

agent = create_tool_calling_agent(llm, tools, system_prompt)

Finally, we can try our agent. Let’s ask about a specific booking and check if the right tool is being called:

agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", 
   "content": "can the booking c3dd03uvulemx15z be canceled?"}]}
)

We can see from the trace breakdown (Figure 7-6) the different steps that are taken. The query starts with an LLM call, which decides to use a tool, executes it, and goes back to the LLM to generate that the booking was successfully canceled, while detailing various other information about that specific booking number.

The details about each input, output, and intermediate results from each step are detailed in the UI you can see in Figure 7-7.

This provides you end-to-end visibility on the process taken inside of your agent for better explainability and debugging purposes.

Testing Tools

It’s important to test your tools when you’re developing AI agents and applications for testing the reliability of these tools. One approach is to leverage unit tests.

Unit testing is a core principle for robust software deployment, and this is true for GenAI projects as well. Tool development benefits from unit tests for key components, such as tool wrappers, API call handlers, and data transformation logic. This helps you ensure that the tools function as expected in most cases. It also reduces the risk of silent failures and makes debugging more efficient before integrating models or deploying agents in production environments.

A second approach is to leverage LLM judges, as we explored in Chapter 6. To use LLM to judge our tools’ performance, we need a proper validation dataset targeted toward our tools. This means that if a query is, “What is the flight schedule for 6 September 2024 in Singapore?,” our validation dataset to this question not only contains the question and expected answer but also:

  • The list of documents expected to answer to this query (vector search tool evaluation)

  • The correct latitude/longitude inputs for Singapore (weather forecast tool evaluation)

  • The correct date inputs for the flights retrieval (database retrieval tool evaluation)

  • The correct set of tools that must be used for this query (orchestrator evaluation)

Having these different sets of information in the validation dataset helps include edge cases and expected failure modes for rigorous assessment. MLflow’s evaluation can then run against these datasets iteratively, applying customized scorers to check whether these assessments are validated in a repeatable way.

For reference, here’s a practical custom scorer to check whether the agent has chosen the right tool for its response. The key here is to have the expected tool in the validation dataset so that the scorer can work properly:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import scorer
from mlflow.genai.judges import meets_guidelines
from typing import Dict, Any

right_tool_usage = """The response must use the correct tool for the response. 
    The expected tool is mentioned in expected_tool which mentions the name of the 
    tool to use."""

@scorer
def right_tool_usage_scorer(inputs: Dict[Any, Any], outputs: Dict[Any, Any], 
    expectations: dict[str, Any]):
       feedbacks = []
       expected_tool = expectations["expected_tool"]

    feedbacks.append(
        meets_guidelines(
            name="Right tool usage",
            guidelines=right_tool_usage,
            context={"response": outputs, "expected_response": expected_tool},
        )
    )
    return feedbacks

This process of evaluating each component of the AI system is crucial for comparing overall agent versions, tracking improvements, and preventing regressions. This can give both developers and stakeholders confidence that quality remains high as the system evolves.

Packaging and Deploying Advanced GenAI Applications with ResponsesAgent

After building and evaluating the agent and its tools, the next step is to prepare the agent for deployment. MLflow provides the ResponsesAgent class, a specialized interface for serving generative AI models that handle structured responses with tool-calling capabilities. This agent is designed to work seamlessly with MLflow’s and Databricks’ serving infrastructure while providing compatibility with OpenAI formatted APIs.

Why and When to Use ResponsesAgent

Using MLflow’s ResponsesAgent is quite beneficial when you need a reliable way to package and deploy generative AI agents, especially those that handle complex tasks such as tool calling and multiturn conversations.

Note

Even though we’ve developed our agent with LangGraph and could use mlflow.langchain to log our model, logging with the MLflow ResponsesAgent class is preferred for deployment purposes due to the structured responses support. Deploying the agent by registering the model with the mlflow.langchain flavor would need a lot of input/output custom functions to be supported by most deployment patterns.

ResponsesAgent organizes inputs and outputs using structured messages (like those in chat applications), tracks model usage, and supports conversation history and metadata for each query. This makes it easy for agents to have features like functions calling, looking up information, and managing ongoing dialogue all within a standardized framework.

The main advantage of ResponsesAgent is its compatibility with any framework the agent is developed in. What ResponseAgent does is wrap the agent code to use OpenAI API specs, meaning you can connect your agent to existing chat UIs or applications that are built for OpenAI’s Responses API or function-calling APIs. There’s no need to rewrite integration code, and you benefit from seamless request and response handling. Let’s see how we can leverage that to pack the agent we’ve just created.

Packaging the Agent with the MLflow ResponsesAgent

To use and customize the MLflow ResponsesAgent class, we start by creating a class for our agent that inherits it. The class will basically wrap around the LangGraph agent we’ve created earlier to customize its predict function when deployed: 

from mlflow.types.responses import ResponsesAgentRequest, ResponsesAgentResponse

class LangGraphResponsesAgent(ResponsesAgent):
    def __init__(self, agent):
        self.agent = agent

    def predict(self, request: ResponsesAgentRequest) -> ResponsesAgentResponse:
        outputs = [
            event.item
            for event in self.predict_stream(request)
            if event.type == "response.output_item.done"
        ]
        return ResponsesAgentResponse(output=outputs, custom_outputs=request.custom_inputs)

Here are the input and output types of the predict function of the MLflow class ResponsesAgent previously defined:

ResponsesAgentRequest (input)

This is a response type provided by MLflow, representing the standardized input for serving agents. It includes fields for structured messages input (e.g., chat history, system, user, assistant roles, tool calls, function arguments), and optional custom_inputs for advanced control and context to be used by the endpoint, which optionally includes conversation_id and user_id.

ResponsesAgentResponse (output)

It contains a list of output items (such as generated responses, tool call results, or streamed tokens), as well as an optional dictionary for custom_outputs that can be used to pass along any additional metadata, evaluation diagnostics, or agent-specific information.

We can also see that the predict function uses a predict_stream function, which streams agent-generated outputs as events. It then filters these for events where event.type == "response.output_item.done", finding the events that are completed responses to return instead of returning partial or intermediate results. Finally, the agent creates a ResponsesAgentResponse object to return, passing the collected outputs and any custom output metadata from the incoming request.

As for the predict_stream method that is in the LangGraphResponsesAgent class, it also takes as input a ResponsesAgentRequest but this time outputs a Generator of ResponsesAgentStreamEvent, as it will yield the response as streaming events.

The main function here that will call the LangGraph agent is the native function self.agent.stream(). Other functions such as _responses_to_cc() and _langchain_to_responses() are functions to help format input and outputs from LangGraph to OpenAI formats. You can find the full class implementation in the GitHub repository. Here is an example:

   def predict_stream(self, request: ResponsesAgentRequest) -> 
           Generator[ResponsesAgentStreamEvent, None, None]:
       cc_msgs = []
       for msg in request.input:
           cc_msgs.extend(self._responses_to_cc(msg.model_dump()))

       for event in self.agent.stream({"messages": cc_msgs}, 
       stream_mode=["updates", "messages"]):
           if event[0] == "updates":
               for node_data in event[1].values():
                   for item in self._langchain_to_responses(node_data["messages"]):
                       yield ResponsesAgentStreamEvent(type="response.output_item.done", 
                       item=item)

           elif event[0] == "messages":
               try:
                   chunk = event[1][0]
                   if isinstance(chunk, AIMessageChunk) and (content := chunk.content):
                       yield ResponsesAgentStreamEvent(
                           **self.create_text_delta(delta=content, item_id=chunk.id),
                       )
               except Exception as e:
                   print(e)

Before we can wrap our LangGraph agent developed earlier into the LangGraph​Res⁠ponsesAgent class, we use mlflow.langchain.autolog() to enable automatic tracing for LangChain and LangGraph components. Now, when the agent runs, MLflow will log artifacts, metrics, and execution traces; this will capture each step, the inputs/outputs, and relevant context for every run.

After we wrap our agent into LangGraphResponsesAgent, we register ⁠the​ responses_agent as the active model within MLflow with mlflow.mod⁠els​.set_model(responses_agent), preparing it for tracking and deployment. By setting the agent this way, MLflow can version it, log additional attributes, and later deploy it:

mlflow.langchain.autolog()
responses_agent = LangGraphResponsesAgent(agent)
mlflow.models.set_model(responses_agent)

Let’s now use the ResponsesAgent wrapped agent (for which you’ll see the response content in the trace shown by Figure 7-8):

result = responses_agent.predict({"input": [{"role": "user", 
    "content": "can the booking c3dd03uvulemx15z be canceled?"}]}
)

Now that our agent is wrapped for deployment, let’s log it with MLflow.

Logging the ResponsesAgent with MLflow

To log our agent for deployment, we first need to take care of authenticating our tools properly. MLflow has modules to set up automatic authentication passthrough. These are in mlflow.models.resources, where we wrap our functions in DatabricksFunction when we want to use tools registered as user-defined functions (UDF) in Unity Catalog, for instance. Other resource types, like vector search or MCP servers, would need other types of MLflow resources. Here is an example: 

from mlflow.models.resources import DatabricksFunction

resources = []
resources.extend(vector_retriever_tool.resources)
resources.extend(DatabricksFunction(function_name=uc_tool.tool_name))

After that, we can specify these resources in the MLflow model logging function, using the resources parameter in mlflow.pyfunc.log_model. This ensures that Databricks automatically configures the needed authentication for each resource during deployment.

Along with logging the agent artifacts, we give our agent a name, and also point python_model to our agent code that is in the agent.py script and add the pip requirements needed for the deployment in pip_requirements:

import mlflow
from importlib.metadata import version
with mlflow.start_run():
    logged_agent_info = mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        name="agent",
        python_model="agent.py",
        pip_requirements=[
            "databricks-langchain",
            f"langgraph=={version('langgraph')}",
            f"backoff=={version('backoff')}",
        ],
        resources=resources,
    )

Before registering the model to Unity Catalog and deploying the agent, it’s always good practice to perform predeployment checks using the function mlflow.​mod⁠els.predict(). This basically simulates the environment building using the recently logged artifacts to load the model and use it. Here is an example:

mlflow.models.predict(
    model_uri=f"runs:/{logged_agent_info.run_id}/agent",
    input_data={"input": [{"role": "user", "content": "Can my battery pack be transported 
        in cabin baggages?"}]},
    env_manager="uv",
)

This usually takes a few minutes, but once it successfully runs, you can have peace of mind that your environment packages are correctly configured.

Register the ResponsesAgent with MLflow in Unity Catalog

Once a model run has created a satisfactory model, we can register that model into the registry. This is done through using the three namespaces nomenclature—the catalog, schema, and model name—before using mlflow.register_model with the agent we just logged earlier. For example: 

mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")

catalog = "workspace"
schema = "unity_airways"
model_name = "unity-airways-booking-agent"
UC_MODEL_NAME = f"{catalog}.{schema}.{model_name}"

# Register the model to UC
uc_registered_model_info = mlflow.register_model(
    model_uri=logged_agent_info.model_uri, name=UC_MODEL_NAME
)

The registered model will appear in the targeted catalog workspace and schema unity_airways, as you can see in Figure 7-9.

Integrating Advanced Capabilities

As you’ve seen, agents are powerful and versatile systems that can be layered to solve complex cases. In this section, we will explore some techniques to continue adding depth to our agents around managing conversation history, the use of MCP servers as external tools, and the integration of agents as tools to drive more powerful, flexible workflows in complex applications.

Context Engineering

Managing context for your GenAI agent can be tricky in practice, especially considering there are many pieces in LLM context to retain, such as:

  • User query and system prompts

  • Conversation history for multiturn conversations

  • Knowledge from other data sources

  • User metadata and preferences

In this section, let’s focus on managing conversation history or often referred to as short-term memory. This is important for creating context-aware AI agents. Conversation history materializes as a list of messages that are ordered by the order of the conversation. A turn in conversation usually refers to a pair of inquiry + response.

We can witness a multiturn conversation of two turns as follows:

[
 {
   "content": "Can the booking c3dd03uvulemx15z be canceled?",
   "type": "human",
 },
 {
   "content": "The booking c3dd03uvulemx15z has been successfully canceled. The 
      decision was approved, and the status is now CANCELED. The coupon status is REFUNDED, 
      and the refunded amount is 126.4. The reason for the cancellation is a standard 
      cancellation approval. If you have any further questions or concerns, please don't 
      hesitate to ask.",
   "type": "ai",
 },
 {
   "content": "What about the booking a3aad03av12345?",
   "type": "human",
 },
 {
   "content": "The booking a3aad03av12345 has already been canceled. If you have any 
      further questions or concerns, please don't hesitate to ask.",
   "type": "ai",
 }
]

This constitutes a conversation history, which would usually be passed to the endpoint for reference so that the agent could realize and incorporate the previous inquiries. The MLflow Trace UI helps retain these conversation turns for easy debugging and understanding of the flow by the agent.

As AI agent endpoints are preferred to remain stateless to be more versatile, the application backend is usually responsible for passing the right conversation history to the endpoint. This is often handled with a database querying the latest conversation turns or history, by identifying the user, while being in session.

LangGraph maintains conversation in the state and sends it to each step of the workflow, but this introduces potential issues where managing context size is crucial: LLMs have a fixed context window, and passing the entire conversation history quickly exceeds these limits, leading to token limit errors or very long latencies.

The conversation history can be manipulated by opening up the messages inside the state being passed across the graph. For instance, in this code snippet of call_model() we used earlier for calling our LLM, we could modify the invoke function to take only the five latest messages in the state instead of the full state, like so:

   def call_model(
       state: AgentState,
       config: RunnableConfig,
   ):
	 recent_messages = {"messages": state["messages"][-5:]} 
       response = model_runnable.invoke(recent_messages, config)
       return {"messages": [response]}

A best practice would be to select only the most relevant parts of the conversation to send, depending on each tool or LLM natures. This approach not only prevents token limit restrictions but also helps focus the model’s attention on what matters most for the current user request and avoid hallucination or misretrieval of information.

Some optimal ways you can pass context to tools include:

  • Passing just the last user query to the tool. This works well for retrieval tools, or text to SQL tools for instance; e.g., “What is the last booking done of this passenger X?”

  • Periodically summarizing earlier interactions and submitting only high-level summaries alongside the most recent dialogue; e.g., “Summary: Passenger X has booked a flight from Sydney to London with booking number A1234. He has been asking about changing his seat number. Here’s the user’s latest input: Can I have an aisle seat?”

  • Or even more advanced is to use an LLM to rephrase the last user query according to the previous conversation. This is useful when queries could be too vague if interpreted standalone; e.g., “Previous input: Passenger X has booked a flight from Sydney to London with booking number A1234. He has asked about changing his seat number. Can I have an aisle seat?” → “Reformulated input: Passenger X requested a seat change for booking number A1234 to an aisle seat.”

There are many possible techniques here that can be applied in applications, depending on what user types will be using the agent. The goal here is to facilitate usage of the application and make its adoption smoother, which starts by understanding how users are to interact with the agent.

Note

Databricks also provides agent memory capabilities that integrate with LangGraph through Databricks Lakebase. A detailed explanation of this functionality is beyond the scope of this book, but there are many good resources out there to choose from, such as Learning LangChain by Mayo Oshin and Nuno Campos (O’Reilly, 2025).

MCP Servers As Tools

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard, open source framework introduced by Anthropic in 2024 to help AI applications access external tools and data sources through standardized protocols. Its popularity comes from its ability to bridge the gap between AI models and many diverse resources. This need became quite trendy with the rise of AI agents, making providers rush to implement and support MCP servers for their products. Some MCP servers wrap around traditional API endpoints or around existing codebase, presenting them in a standardized format that is easier for LLM models and agent frameworks to handle, as Figure 7-10 illustrates.

As for the offering of MCP servers integration, a key distinction exists between managed MCP servers and external MCP servers:

  • Managed MCP servers are typically hosted and maintained by a cloud provider or platform (such as Databricks), offering secure defaults, built-in authentication, automatic scalability, and centralized updates. They are out-of-the-box solutions, enabling teams to access specific services without the burden of development or infrastructure deployment.

  • In contrast, external MCP servers refer to those hosted by either your organization or a third-party provider, outside the managed platform. These external deployments offer maximum flexibility, allowing for custom configuration and potential integration with proprietary data or unique tools, but come with extra responsibilities around server maintenance, access control, and implementation efforts.

The choice between managed and external MCP servers often depends on your team’s need for control versus convenience, as well as your particular security and compliance requirements. In our example, we will leverage Databricks-managed MCP server to call our Vector Search index:

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient

workspace_client = WorkspaceClient()
host = workspace_client.config.host
MANAGED_MCP_SERVER_URL = f"{host}/api/2.0/mcp/vector-search/workspace/unity_airways"

First, we configure our workspace client for authentication and add the right URL to call the Databricks-managed MCP server for vector search. URLs for managed MCP servers can usually be found in the documentation of the provider you’re interested in. We fill in workspace/unity_airways at the end of the URL as documented, to point to the schema in Unity Catalog where our Vector Search index resides.

Next, we can start building our MCP server tool integration. We create the class MCPTool that inherits the BaseTool class of LangChain. This class is mainly to add authentication and wrap the call of the MCP server of Databricks into a LangChain compatible one, as we can see in the run function:

from databricks_mcp import DatabricksMCPClient
from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool

class MCPTool(BaseTool):
    def __init__(
        self,
        name: str,
        description: str,
        args_schema: type,
        server_url: str,
        ws: WorkspaceClient,
    ):
        super().__init__(name=name, description=description, args_schema=args_schema)
        object.__setattr__(self, "server_url", server_url)
        object.__setattr__(self, "workspace_client", ws)

    def _run(self, **kwargs) -> str:
        """Execute the MCP tool"""
        mcp_client = DatabricksMCPClient(
            server_url=self.server_url, workspace_client=self.workspace_client
        )
        response = mcp_client.call_tool(self.name, kwargs)
        return "".join([c.text for c in response.content])

Then, we need a function to instantiate the LangChain BaseTool class we’ve just created. This function mainly reads Databricks’ MCP server properties and rearranges them into the newly created class MCPTool. It also creates a type mapping using the expected input of the MCP server and formalizes it into the class MCPTool through the pydantic function create_model():

from pydantic import create_model

# Convert an MCP tool definition into a LangChain-compatible tool
def create_langchain_tool_from_mcp(
    mcp_tool, server_url: str, ws: WorkspaceClient
):
    """Create a LangChain tool from an MCP tool definition"""
    schema = mcp_tool.inputSchema.copy()
    properties = schema.get("properties", {})
    required = schema.get("required", [])

    # Map JSON schema types to Python types for input validation
    TYPE_MAPPING = {"integer": int, "number": float, "boolean": bool}
    field_definitions = {}
    for field_name, field_info in properties.items():
        field_type_str = field_info.get("type", "string")
        field_type = TYPE_MAPPING.get(field_type_str, str)

        if field_name in required:
            field_definitions[field_name] = (field_type, ...)
        else:
            field_definitions[field_name] = (field_type, None)

    # Dynamically create a Pydantic schema for the tool's input arguments
    args_schema = create_model(f"{mcp_tool.name}Args", **field_definitions)

    # Return a configured MCPTool instance
    return MCPTool(
        name=mcp_tool.name,
        description=mcp_tool.description or f"Tool: {mcp_tool.name}",
        args_schema=args_schema,
        server_url=server_url,
        ws=ws
        )

Finally, we can create our Databricks MCP server tools mcp_tools and pass them to our function to transform it into a LangChain MCPTool object mcp_langchain_tool:

mcp_tools = DatabricksMCPClient(server_url=MANAGED_MCP_SERVER_URL, 
   workspace_client=workspace_client).list_tools()
mcp_langchain_tool = create_langchain_tool_from_mcp(mcp_tools[0], 
   MANAGED_MCP_SERVER_URL, workspace_client)

Now, let’s try it:

mcp_langchain_tool.run(tool_input={"query": "What are the amenities in the plane?"})

This will start the execution of the tool with respect to the query. You can see the tool output appear within the MLflow Trace UI in Figure 7-11.

After that, we can integrate this tool directly, as we’ve done previously in the chapter. Using MCP servers rather than API is a good way to uniformize your tool-calling implementations and make them more robust.

Multiagents Orchestration and Agents As Tools

Let’s imagine our user, who is now aware of their schedule and wants to move their flight to another day but doesn’t know which one yet. To help them with their decision, we could offer them flight recommendations. Thankfully, we already have an in-house flight recommender model for our website. We can add this agent specialized in flight recommendation as a tool to our GenAI application. As our other agent is deployed in an API endpoint, it is quite easy to call and create the code to execute it with the latest state of the conversation:

from databricks_langchain import ChatDatabricks
FLIGHT_RECOMMENDER_ENDPOINT = "flight_recommender_agent_endpoint"

def get_flight_recommendation(state):
       # Extract the latest user query
       user_msg = state[-1:]

       # Build system-augmented prompt
       flight_agent = ChatDatabricks(endpoint=FLIGHT_RECOMMENDER_ENDPOINT)
       response = flight_agent.invoke(user_msg)
       messages = []
       for message in response.content:
           if message.get("role") == "assistant":
               messages.append(message)

       return {"messages": messages}

We then use the Tool class to create the tool. And we can then integrate it to the AI agent as we’ve done earlier with our previous tools:

from langchain.tools import Tool

flight_recommendation_tool = Tool(
    name="flight_recommendation_agent",
    func=get_flight_recommendation,
    description="Get real time flight recommendation according to the user input.",
)

With these building blocks in place, you can extend your agent with additional tools and capabilities.

Conclusion and Key Takeaways

In this chapter, we explored the fundamental challenges of building AI agents with MLflow. After reading this, you should have a strong understanding of how to enhance your AI systems with the right tools, from database connectors and API-based search to dynamic code execution.

The case study example showed you:

  • How to use LangChain and LangGraph frameworks along with MLflow to let you wrap functions as agent tools, and create clear and purpose-specific definitions for tools.

  • How to integrate tools with an agent with LangGraph and MLflow ResponsesAgent.

  • How to leverage MLflow evaluation to validate proper performance of the tools and agent.

  • More advanced topics and best practices around conversation history management, using agents as tools and connecting to MCP servers for scalable workflows.

Together, these approaches enable you to build production-ready AI solutions that are flexible, resilient, and maintainable over time.

This chapter walked through building, testing, and orchestrating agentic workflows one step at a time. In your own practice, start small. Add tools incrementally, evaluate each component, and move toward deployment only after the pieces work well on their own. MLflow gives you the tracking and evaluation infrastructure to do this with confidence.
